title: How Much Water Should I Drink a Day? Calculator + Chart | Hacé Cuentas
h1: How Much Water Should You Drink Per Day? (By Body Weight)
description: How much water should you drink a day? Enter your weight to get your target in liters, fl oz, and cups. Free, no sign-up needed and instant results.
answerSnippet: A simple rule: drink **35 ml per kg of body weight** per day. For a 154 lb (70 kg) adult, that is **2.45 L (83 fl oz / ~10 cups)**. Add 600 ml per hour of exercise, 500 ml for hot climates, and 500–700 ml for pregnancy or breastfeeding. The NAM Adequate Intake is 3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women (total water, including food).
intro:
How much water do you actually need per day? The short answer depends on your weight, how much you move, and where you live. This calculator uses the **35 ml per kg** baseline established by the National Academies of Medicine (NAM) Dietary Reference Intakes, then layers in evidence-based adjustments for exercise (ACSM: ~600 ml per training hour), hot or humid climates (+500 ml), pregnancy (+500 ml), and lactation (+700 ml).

The NAM Adequate Intake (AI) — the level assumed sufficient for nearly all healthy people — is **3.7 L/day (~125 oz) for men** and **2.7 L/day (~91 oz) for women**, but roughly 20% of that comes from food. Individual sweat rate matters more than any formula: outdoor athletes in heat can lose up to **1.5 L per hour**, while a sedentary office worker in AC barely cracks 500 ml of insensible loss. Use the result as a daily target, not a prescription.
keyTakeaway: A 154 lb (70 kg) sedentary adult in a temperate climate needs roughly 2.45 liters (83 oz / ~10 cups) of fluid per day; one hour of training adds ~600 mL, and hot weather adds another 500 mL — match the trend, not the decimal.
useCases: Athlete planning training-day fluid intake (baseline + 12–16 oz per training hour, electrolytes >60 min)
Post-illness rehydration after fever, vomiting, or diarrhea (add 500 mL per °F above 100.4°F)
Pregnancy hydration target per NAM (+300–500 mL above non-pregnant AI; ~3.0 L total water/day)
Kidney stone prevention per AUA guideline (aim for 2.5+ L urine output, often 3+ L total fluid intake)
Breastfeeding mothers producing ~750 mL milk/day (+700 mL fluid above baseline)
Outdoor workers in hot climates tracking heat-stress hydration
Older adults with diminished thirst sensation setting structured fluid reminders
Weight-loss clients replacing caloric beverages with water

outputs.label: Daily Water Target (8 fl oz Cups)

explanation:
## Quick-reference table: daily water by body weight

The baseline formula is **35 ml × weight in kg** (or 0.5 fl oz × weight in lb). The table below shows sedentary intake in a temperate climate (no exercise, no climate or pregnancy add-ons):

| Weight (lb) | Weight (kg) | Liters/day | Fl oz/day | Cups/day |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 110 lb | 50 kg | **1.75 L** | 59 oz | ~7.4 cups |
| 130 lb | 59 kg | **2.07 L** | 70 oz | ~8.7 cups |
| 150 lb | 68 kg | **2.38 L** | 80 oz | ~10 cups |
| 154 lb | 70 kg | **2.45 L** | 83 oz | ~10.4 cups |
| 175 lb | 79 kg | **2.77 L** | 94 oz | ~11.7 cups |
| 200 lb | 91 kg | **3.19 L** | 108 oz | ~13.5 cups |
| 220 lb | 100 kg | **3.50 L** | 118 oz | ~14.8 cups |
| 250 lb | 113 kg | **3.97 L** | 134 oz | ~16.7 cups |

**Add-ons on top of the base:** +600 ml per hour of exercise · +500 ml for hot/humid climate · +500 ml if pregnant · +700 ml if breastfeeding.

## NAM Dietary Reference Intakes: the actual numbers

The National Academies of Medicine (NAM) Adequate Intake (AI) — the level assumed to meet the needs of nearly all healthy people:

| Group | Total water AI | From beverages | From food |
|---|---|---|---|
| Men 19+ | **3.7 L/day (~125 oz)** | 3.0 L (~13 cups) | 0.7 L (~24 oz) |
| Women 19+ | **2.7 L/day (~91 oz)** | 2.2 L (~9 cups) | 0.5 L (~17 oz) |
| Pregnancy | 3.0 L/day | 2.3 L | 0.7 L |
| Lactation | 3.8 L/day | 3.1 L | 0.7 L |

About **20% of daily water comes from food** — watermelon is 92% water, cucumber 95%, soup ~90%, leafy greens 90+%, yogurt ~85%. So a man hitting the NAM AI by drinking 13 cups of pure water and eating a typical mixed diet is technically over-target.

## Does coffee dehydrate you? No.

Maughan's 2016 Beverage Hydration Index meta-analysis (American Journal of Clinical Nutrition) ranked drinks by 2-hour fluid retention vs. still water. Milk, oral rehydration solution, and orange juice scored *higher* than plain water; coffee and tea scored essentially equal to water at typical serving sizes (~3 mg/kg caffeine). The diuretic effect of caffeine is real but small and offset by the fluid volume of the beverage. **Bottom line:** coffee, tea, milk, juice, and even diet soda count toward the AI for healthy adults.

## The 0.5–1 oz per lb rule explained

The rule has no formal endorsement, but it cross-checks well against NAM. A 200 lb active man → 100–200 oz → 3.0–5.9 L, which spans the NAM AI (3.7 L) plus exercise replacement. For sedentary adults, **0.5 oz/lb** is enough; **1 oz/lb** is reserved for hard-training athletes, hot climates, or large body sizes. Use it as a sanity check, not gospel.

## Athlete protocols: Galpin baseline + ACSM electrolytes

Andy Galpin's working protocol for athletes: **0.5 oz × body weight in lb as baseline**, then **12–16 oz of fluid per hour of training**. The American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand on Exercise and Fluid Replacement adds the electrolyte layer — for sessions over 60 minutes, replace **sodium 500–700 mg/L, potassium 80–200 mg/L** of fluid. Sweat sodium concentration ranges 600–1,200 mg/L (heavy salty sweaters trend higher), potassium 200–700 mg/L, magnesium 100–300 mg/L. Plain water for >1 hour endurance without electrolytes is the classic setup for **exercise-associated hyponatremia** (serum Na <135 mmol/L) — rare but potentially fatal. Marathon runners drinking >1 L/hour of pure water are the textbook case.

## Hydration assessment: WUT and urine color

Three simple field markers (the WUT check):
- **Weight** loss >2% body weight after exercise = significant dehydration
- **Urine** color pale straw (1–3 on the 8-point chart) = well hydrated; dark amber (5+) = drink up
- **Thirst** is a reliable signal for healthy sedentary adults (Phillips 1984) but **blunted in older adults** and during intense exercise

Urine specific gravity (USG) **<1.020** is the lab-grade marker of euhydration; >1.030 signals dehydration.

## Clinical exceptions — when more isn't better

- **Chronic kidney disease (CKD)** stages 4–5 and **heart failure** often require fluid restriction (typically 1.5–2 L/day) — follow your nephrologist or cardiologist
- **Hyponatremia history** or SIADH — individualized targets, often lower
- **Kidney stone prevention** — the AUA Medical Management of Kidney Stones guideline recommends **>2.5 L of urine output daily**, which usually means **3+ L total fluid intake**
- **Fever** — add ~500 mL per °F above 100.4°F
- **Altitude** above 8,000 ft — add 500 mL until acclimatized (3–5 days)

Thirst, urine color, and how you feel during the day are still the best real-time gauges. The number this calculator gives you is a starting target — adjust based on what your body tells you.

faq.q: How much water should I drink per day based on my weight?
faq.a: The standard evidence-based baseline is **35 ml per kg of body weight** (roughly 0.5 fl oz per pound). For a 154 lb (70 kg) adult, that is about 2.45 liters (83 fl oz / ~10 cups) per day in a temperate climate with no exercise. Add 600 ml for each hour of training, 500 ml for hot or humid weather, 500 ml if pregnant, or 700 ml if breastfeeding. The NAM Adequate Intake is 3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women including water from food.

faq.q: Is the '8 glasses a day' rule accurate?
faq.a: Mostly not. The 64 oz / 1.9 L figure has no clear scientific origin and undershoots the NAM Adequate Intake of 3.7 L for men and 2.7 L for women (total water, including food). It is a memorable rule of thumb that happens to be roughly right for a small sedentary woman in cool weather — and roughly wrong for almost everyone else. Body weight, activity, and climate matter more than any fixed glass count.

faq.q: Does coffee count toward my daily water intake?
faq.a: Yes. Maughan's 2016 Beverage Hydration Index (AJCN) found coffee at typical doses (~3 mg/kg caffeine) retains fluid essentially the same as plain water over 2 hours. The mild diuretic effect of caffeine is offset by the volume of liquid in the beverage. Coffee, tea, milk, and juice all count toward your daily total.

faq.q: What does healthy urine color look like?
faq.a: Pale straw to light yellow — like lemonade with extra ice. That is 1 to 3 on the 8-point urine color chart used in sports medicine. Dark amber (5+) means drink more. Completely clear may signal overhydration, especially if you are urinating every 30 minutes. First-morning urine is normally darker after 7–8 hours without fluid — judge color mid-day.

faq.q: Do I need to drink extra water when exercising?
faq.a: Yes. The ACSM recommends replacing sweat losses during and after exercise — roughly 600 ml (about 20 oz) per hour of moderate activity as a starting estimate. For sessions over 60 minutes or in heat, add electrolytes (500–700 mg sodium per liter). Weigh yourself before and after a workout: every pound lost equals roughly 480 ml (16 oz) of fluid deficit to replace.

faq.q: How much water should pregnant women drink per day?
faq.a: The NAM raises total water intake to 3.0 L/day during pregnancy (an extra ~300–500 mL above the 2.7 L baseline) and 3.8 L/day during lactation (+1.1 L). The lactation bump is driven by milk production: breast milk is 87% water and a typical day produces 750–800 mL. Match thirst plus the modest add-on — extremely high targets are generally not evidence-based.

faq.q: Do foods like watermelon and cucumber count as water intake?
faq.a: Yes — and the NAM AI already assumes about 20% of daily water comes from food. Watermelon is 92% water, cucumber 95%, lettuce 96%, strawberries 91%, yogurt 85%, cooked oatmeal 84%. A salad-heavy lunch can contribute 300–500 mL of water. Soups are a particularly efficient hydration vehicle.

faq.q: When should I use a sports drink instead of plain water?
faq.a: For sessions under 60 minutes at moderate intensity in a temperate environment, plain water is fine. For longer sessions, high-intensity work, hot environments, or heavy sweaters, electrolyte replacement matters — aim for 500–700 mg sodium per liter of fluid per ACSM. A DIY sports drink: 1 L water + 1/4 tsp salt + 2 tbsp sugar. Plain water only for >1 hour endurance work sets up exercise-associated hyponatremia in rare cases.

faq.q: Can drinking too much water be dangerous?
faq.a: Yes, though it is uncommon in everyday life. Exercise-associated hyponatremia (serum sodium <135 mmol/L) results from overdrinking plain water, most often in marathon and triathlon runners consuming >1 L/hour with no electrolytes. Healthy kidneys handle about 0.8–1.0 L/hour of free water. Normal daily totals from this calculator (2–4 L/day spread out) are safe for healthy adults. People with CKD, heart failure, or SIADH should follow clinician guidance on fluid limits.

faq.q: How much water should older adults drink?
faq.a: The same baseline by weight applies, but thirst sensation declines with age (Phillips 1984) so older adults often under-drink even when they need fluid. Setting a structured schedule — a glass with each meal, one mid-morning, one mid-afternoon, one with medications — works better than relying on thirst. Note that diuretics, lithium, and SGLT-2 inhibitors all change fluid balance and may require adjusted targets.

faq.q: How much water should I drink to help prevent kidney stones?
faq.a: The American Urological Association Medical Management of Kidney Stones guideline recommends maintaining urine output of at least 2.5 L per day, which usually requires 3+ L of total fluid intake. Spread intake through the day — slamming water before bed is less effective. Citrate-rich fluids (lemon water, orange juice) add a secondary benefit by raising urinary citrate, which inhibits calcium oxalate crystals.

referenceTables.title: Water content of common foods (the ~20% you don't have to drink)
referenceTables.caption: The NAM Adequate Intake assumes roughly 20% of daily water comes from food. These percentages (USDA FoodData Central) show why a salad-and-fruit-heavy day quietly covers 300–800 mL of your target. The 'water per typical serving' column converts the percentage into millilitres so you can subtract it from the number this calculator gives you.
referenceTables.note: Percentages are approximate USDA FoodData Central values for raw/cooked foods and vary by ripeness and preparation. Coffee, tea, milk and juice also count toward fluid intake (Beverage Hydration Index, AJCN 2016) — only alcohol has a net dehydrating effect at higher doses.

referenceTables.title: NAM Adequate Intake for total water, by age and sex
referenceTables.caption: The National Academies of Medicine set these Adequate Intake (AI) values for TOTAL water — beverages plus food. They are population targets, not personal prescriptions; the calculator above scales by your body weight, which is usually a closer fit for an individual.
referenceTables.note: Source: National Academies of Medicine, Dietary Reference Intakes for Water (2005). About 20% of these totals normally comes from food, so the beverage-only target is roughly 80% of the figures shown.
